al-sufi-andromeda-964.hook: A little cloud in his star book was another galaxy
lines: In 964 the Persian astronomer Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi finished his Book of Fixed Stars in Isfahan.
He checked every star in Ptolemy's catalogue with his own eyes, and in Andromeda he described a small cloud.
It is the earliest known record of the Andromeda galaxy, which no one understood as separate until the 1920s.
al-sufi-andromeda-964.caption:
Al-Sufi went through Ptolemy's catalogue constellation by constellation and drew each one twice, as seen on a globe and as seen in the sky. He also wrote down the Arabic names Bedouin observers were already using. His book was copied and translated for six hundred years, and many star names in use today come through it.

ibn-al-shatir-copernicus.hook: A mosque timekeeper's lunar model matches Copernicus exactly
lines: Ibn al-Shatir kept the prayer times at the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus and built the sundial for its minaret.
In 1957 Victor Roberts showed his model of the moon is identical to the one Copernicus published in 1543.
No Latin translation of Ibn al-Shatir is known, Copernicus never names him, and no route between them has been found.
ibn-al-shatir-copernicus.caption:
Ibn al-Shatir rebuilt planetary astronomy out of uniform circular motions alone, discarding Ptolemy's equant and off centre circles. Victor Roberts worked with E. S. Kennedy in Beirut, and found that several parameters match as well. Some scholars argue for transmission through Byzantine Greek manuscripts, others for two men solving the same problem the same way. One difference is plain: Ibn al-Shatir kept the earth at the centre, and Copernicus moved it.

qalawun-hospital-1284.hook: A Cairo hospital was endowed to turn nobody away
lines: The Mamluk sultan Qalawun founded a hospital in Cairo in 1284, on the site of a former Fatimid palace.
Its endowment deed survives, setting out separate wards, a pharmacy, a library and a salaried staff of physicians.
Payment was never required of the patient, and the site has served the sick almost continuously since.
qalawun-hospital-1284.caption:
The deed also provided for oculists and surgeons, and for an allowance paid on discharge to sick people who could not work. Qalawun's complex held a school and his tomb as well as the hospital. Endowed hospitals of this kind, called bimaristans, existed across the Muslim world from the ninth century, and an eye hospital still operates on the Cairo site.

ibn-al-nafis-circulation-1242.hook: He corrected Galen on the heart and was lost for centuries
lines: Around 1242 in Cairo, the Syrian physician Ibn al-Nafis wrote on the anatomy in Ibn Sina's Canon.
He held that the wall of the heart is solid, and that blood must go from the right chamber to the lungs and back.
That is the pulmonary circulation, described three centuries before European anatomists.
ibn-al-nafis-circulation-1242.caption:
The accepted view, from Galen and from Ibn Sina alike, was that blood crossed from the right side of the heart to the left through invisible pores. Ibn al-Nafis wrote that there are no pores, and that the blood mixes with air in the lungs. His text then sat unread until a physician, Muhyi al-Din al-Tatawi, found it in a Berlin manuscript and published on it in 1924.

al-jazari-machines-1206.hook: An engineer drew about fifty machines and how to build them
lines: In 1206, at the Artuqid court in Diyarbakir, al-Jazari finished his Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices.
It sets out about fifty machines with exploded diagrams and step by step instructions, from water clocks to pumps.
He wrote that he would describe nothing he had not built and tested himself. He died the year the book was completed.
al-jazari-machines-1206.caption:
Among the machines are an elephant clock combining Indian, Greek, Chinese and Arab parts, hand washing basins that pour and refill, and musical automata. Historians of technology point to his use of the crankshaft joined to a connecting rod, and of segmental gears and a camshaft, in machines that actually worked.

tusi-couple.hook: Two rolling circles turn a circle into a straight line
lines: Ptolemy's models needed the equant, a point about which a planet swept equal angles though it was not the centre.
In 1247 Nasir al-Din al-Tusi rolled a small circle inside a circle of twice its diameter, tracing a straight line.
Circular motions alone can therefore produce oscillation, and the construction is called the Tusi couple.
tusi-couple.caption:
The equant predicted well and it broke the rule that motion in the heavens is uniform and circular, so astronomers had complained about it for centuries. Al-Tusi's answer removed the need for it. The same construction appears, drawn the same way and with no attribution, in Copernicus's book of 1543, and how it got there is a standing question.

al-battani-solar-year.hook: He measured the year and was off by two minutes
lines: Al-Battani observed from Raqqa, on the Euphrates, from about 877 until 918, with instruments he had built himself.
He put the solar year at 365 days, 5 hours, 46 minutes and 24 seconds, about two minutes and twenty seconds short.
His tables were translated into Latin in the twelfth century, and Copernicus cites him repeatedly in the book of 1543.
al-battani-solar-year.caption:
Al-Battani also found that the point at which the sun is furthest from the earth had shifted since Ptolemy recorded its position, which meant the Greek tables were not simply to be copied forward. In Europe he was known as Albategnius. There is a crater on the moon carrying his Latin name.

fatima-al-fihri-qarawiyyin.hook: She spent her inheritance on a mosque that has never closed
lines: Fatima al-Fihri's family migrated from Kairouan to Fez in the early ninth century.
When her father died she spent her share of his estate on a mosque, built in 859, in the migrants' quarter.
That mosque, al-Qarawiyyin, gathered teaching circles, then a library, then salaried professors, and never closed.
fatima-al-fihri-qarawiyyin.caption:
Al-Qarawiyyin issued certificates to those who studied there, and UNESCO and Guinness both list it as the oldest existing degree granting institution. Tradition holds that Fatima fasted while the building work went on. Almost everything told about her comes from Ibn Abi Zar's chronicle, written some five centuries later, and historians say plainly that earlier evidence for her life is thin.

al-razi-case-records.hook: Al-Razi wrote down the cases where he was wrong
lines: Abu Bakr al-Razi was born in Rayy, near modern Tehran, and ran hospitals there and in Baghdad.
His case notes record particular patients, the treatment given and whether it worked, including the times it did not.
He argued that medicine advances only when a physician trusts a careful observation over a great name.
al-razi-case-records.caption:
The Hawi, the book al-Razi is best known for, was not written by him for readers. His students assembled it after his death from his working notebooks, which is why it reads as it does: an authority quoted, then Greek and Indian opinion, then a mark meaning mine, followed by what he had seen at the bedside. His book of doubts about Galen held that Galen's own method demanded exactly that.

ulugh-beg-catalogue-1437.hook: A governor remeasured the sky and catalogued 1,018 stars
lines: In the 1420s Ulugh Beg, governor of Samarkand, built an observatory around a sextant arc about forty metres in radius.
In 1437 his team completed the Zij-i Sultani, a catalogue of 1,018 stars measured fresh, not copied from Ptolemy.
Their value for the length of the year is within about a minute of the modern figure.
ulugh-beg-catalogue-1437.caption:
The great arc was sunk into a trench cut in the rock so that it could not shift. Ulugh Beg was a grandson of Timur, and by all accounts more interested in the sky than in ruling. He was killed in 1449, and the buried arc of his instrument was rediscovered by excavation in 1908 and can be visited today.

zubayda-pilgrim-road-831.hook: A caliph's wife paid for the water on the Makkah road
lines: Zubayda bint Ja'far, wife of Harun al-Rashid, made the hajj and saw pilgrims dying of thirst on the way.
She spent her own fortune on wells, cisterns, paved stretches and waystations along some 1,500 kilometres of desert.
The route has been called Darb Zubayda, Zubayda's Road, ever since.
zubayda-pilgrim-road-831.caption:
Her wells were not the end of it. Zubayda also paid for a spring channel at Makkah that carried water into the city itself, and the remains of her pools and milestones are still mapped across Iraq and Saudi Arabia. She died in 831, and her name survived not through a battle or a dynasty but through drinking water.

timbuktu-manuscripts-rescue-2013.hook: Timbuktu's manuscripts were smuggled out in footlockers
lines: Armed groups took Timbuktu in 2012, and its libraries held centuries of work on law, astronomy and medicine.
The librarian Abdel Kader Haidara organised an evacuation by car, donkey and boat down the Niger, past checkpoints.
By early 2013 an estimated 350,000 manuscripts had reached houses in Bamako.
timbuktu-manuscripts-rescue-2013.caption:
Many of these manuscripts had never left the families who copied them, and they cover law, astronomy, medicine, poetry and mathematics. Volunteers packed them into metal footlockers and rice sacks and moved them a few at a time. Some were burned in Timbuktu, but far fewer than first reported, and the collections are now being conserved and digitised in the south of the country.

astrolabe-model-of-the-sky.hook: An astrolabe is a model of the sky, held in the hand
astrolabe-model-of-the-sky.date: Oldest dated example by Nastulus · 927 CE
lines: A star or the sun is sighted through the bar on the back, and its height above the horizon is read off the rim.
Turning the openwork grid on the front until it matches gives the time of day or night, with no arithmetic needed.
Muslim makers turned it into a standard object, engraved with prayer times and the direction of Makkah.
astrolabe-model-of-the-sky.caption:
The geometry behind it is Greek: flattening the sphere of the sky onto a disc goes back to Hipparchus. The same instrument gives the direction being faced, where any other star has got to, and the height of the tower across the street. Chaucer wrote a manual for one in English, for his ten year old son.

banu-musa-ingenious-devices.hook: Three brothers designed machines that regulated themselves
lines: Muhammad, Ahmad and al-Hasan, the sons of Musa ibn Shakir, were astronomers in ninth century Baghdad.
Around 850 they produced the Book of Ingenious Devices, about a hundred machines that mostly look like toys.
The surprise is a hidden control: a float rises with the liquid and closes a valve, holding a condition steady.
banu-musa-ingenious-devices.caption:
That is feedback, a machine keeping a condition steady with no hand on it: a siphon that empties a chamber at a set level, a lamp that trims its own wick and draws up its own oil. The brothers were patrons as well as builders, paying translators out of their own pockets. Their book also describes a grab for lifting objects off a riverbed, and Donald Hill translated it into English in 1979.

block-printed-amulets-fustat.hook: Arabic was printed on paper before printing existed in Europe
lines: They are narrow strips of paper carrying Qur'anic verses and prayers, rolled into metal amulet cases.
About sixty survive, printed from carved blocks, most of them dug up at Fustat, the old settlement under Cairo.
The trade stayed with street sellers and never moved to books, and historians still disagree about why.
block-printed-amulets-fustat.caption:
The strips come from medieval Egypt and Syria and date from roughly the tenth to the fourteenth centuries. Printing on paper was practised in Arabic long before it existed in Europe, yet it stayed confined to amulets sold in the street, a trade of low standing. Historians give various reasons, from the prestige of the copyist's hand to the economics of a strong manuscript trade, and none of them is settled.

hijri-calendar-epoch-622.hook: The Muslim year counts from a departure, not a birth
hijri-calendar-epoch-622.date: Set under Umar ibn al-Khattab · c. 638 CE
lines: Around 638 CE the caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab and his advisers had to decide where the Muslim calendar should begin.
They chose the Hijra, the migration from Makkah to Yathrib, and the first day of year 1 falls on 16 July 622.
Every Islamic date since is counted from a group of refugees arriving in a town that agreed to take them in.
hijri-calendar-epoch-622.caption:
The choice was deliberate. Umar and his advisers passed over the birth of the Prophet ﷺ, the first revelation and every victory, and took the migration instead, because that was when a scattered community became a society with obligations to one another. By the standard reckoning that day, the first of Muharram in year 1, falls in the Julian calendar.

constitution-of-medina-622.hook: Medina's founding document named Jews as part of one community
lines: Soon after arriving in Yathrib in 622, the Prophet ﷺ set out the terms on which a mixed town would live.
The early biographer Ibn Ishaq preserved it: it names the tribes and puts the Jewish clans in one community.
Historians treat it as one of the earliest written constitutional documents anywhere.
constitution-of-medina-622.caption:
The document is usually called the Sahifa, or Constitution of Medina. It states that the listed clans form one community alongside the believers, guarantees them their religion, fixes who pays blood money for whom, requires joint defence of the town, and sends disputes to arbitration rather than feud. It was written for a place with more than one faith in it.

zakat-is-growth.hook: The word for alms means growth, not deduction
zakat-is-growth.date: Root z k w, growth and purity
lines: Zakat is the obligatory portion of accumulated wealth handed over each year.
Its root z k w means to grow and to increase, and also to be pure, and the noun is used of a plant that thrives.
So the term for taking a fortieth out of savings is a word about the pile getting larger.
zakat-is-growth.caption:
Arabic takes purity and increase from the same three letters because a thing cleaned of what spoils it grows better. The Qur'an uses the same verb of the self in the chapter of the sun: he has succeeded who causes it to grow, and he has failed who buries it. One verb covers a bank balance and a person.

longest-verse-is-a-contract.hook: The longest verse in the Qur'an is about debt
lines: Verse 282 of Surah al-Baqarah is the longest single verse in the Qur'an, longer than most of the short chapters.
It is a commercial instruction: when a debt is contracted for a fixed term, write it down and bring witnesses.
The most space given to any one subject goes to keeping an accurate record of what one person owes another.
longest-verse-is-a-contract.caption:
The verse is not about prayer or paradise. It asks for a scribe to write justly, tells the one who owes to dictate, allows for a debtor who cannot dictate, and permits a pledge instead of a written record when travelling. It also says the writing down should not be thought beneath anyone, whether the sum is small or large.

lines: Each canonical reading comes through named students, usually two, so ten readings arrive as twenty transmissions.

lines: The Qur'an states that the number of months with Allah is twelve, and that four of them are sacred.

ring-composition.hook: Some chapters are built as a ring around a centre

cave-of-thawr-hijra.hook: The cave in the Qur'an held two men for three nights
lines: Jabal Thawr rises south of Makkah, higher and harder to climb than Jabal al-Nour.
In 622 the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr hid in a cave near its summit for three nights while Quraysh combed the roads north.

Only then did they set out for Yathrib by a coastal route. The familiar detail of a spider's web and nesting doves across the entrance comes from later biographical literature, not from the Qur'an, and hadith scholars have long noted that its chains are weak.

mount-uhud-madinah.hook: A mountain the Prophet said loves us and we love it
mount-uhud-madinah.date: Jabal Uhud, Madinah · battle 3 AH, 625 CE
lines: Uhud is a red granite ridge a few kilometres north of the Prophet's mosque, standing apart from the ranges around it.
The battle at its foot in 625 cost the Muslims about seventy dead, after archers left the hill they were told to hold.
Bukhari and Muslim record the Prophet ﷺ saying of it that this is a mountain that loves us and we love it.
mount-uhud-madinah.caption:
The name, meaning single or alone, is usually traced to the ridge standing apart. The Prophet's uncle Hamza was among the dead. The archers' hill, Jabal al-Rumat, is still there, a rise of a few metres beside the cemetery of the fallen.

badr-wells-on-the-caravan-road.hook: Badr was a watering stop on the road to Syria
lines: Badr lies about 130 kilometres southwest of Madinah, near the caravan route to Syria, and it had wells.
Whoever held the wells chose where an army could stand, and on 17 Ramadan of year 2 the Muslims reached them first.
The whole engagement turned on water in a dry valley.
badr-wells-on-the-caravan-road.caption:
The smaller Muslim force filled in the rest of the wells. The place is an ordinary town today, with a mosque, a museum and a walled graveyard holding the fourteen Muslims who died in the battle. Historians still argue about exactly which depressions in the ground were the wells.

aqsa-compound-fourteen-hectares.hook: Al-Aqsa is the whole enclosure, not only the silver dome
lines: In Muslim usage al-Masjid al-Aqsa names the entire walled enclosure in Jerusalem, about fourteen and a half hectares.
It includes the Dome of the Rock, the silver domed hall at the southern end, courtyards, fountains and cisterns.
The Qur'an calls it the farthest mosque in the verse about the Prophet ﷺ being taken by night.
aqsa-compound-fourteen-hectares.caption:
The congregational hall has been destroyed and rebuilt repeatedly, mainly by earthquakes: the shocks of 748 and 1033 each brought much of it down, and its present columns and arcades are largely eleventh century work with Fatimid, Crusader, Ayyubid and modern repairs on top. umayyad-mosque-damascus-layers.hook: Four religions built on the same rectangle in Damascus
lines: The Great Mosque of Damascus stands inside a walled rectangle that began as an Aramean temple precinct to Hadad.
It became a Roman temple of Jupiter, and by the fourth century held a Christian basilica of John the Baptist.
After the conquest of 635 the two communities used parts of the site alongside each other for about seventy years.
umayyad-mosque-damascus-layers.caption:
In 705 the caliph al-Walid took over the church and built the mosque that stands now, finished around 715. Sources differ on the terms, some reporting compensation and other churches given in exchange, others plain seizure. A shrine inside is said to hold the head of John the Baptist, and Christian as well as Muslim visitors still stop at it.

cordoba-mezquita-arches.hook: Cordoba's double arches made short columns carry a high roof
lines: Abd al-Rahman I began the mosque of Cordoba in 785 on the site of a church, first shared and then bought.
His builders had Roman and Visigothic columns too short for the roof they wanted, so they stacked two arches on each.
It worked, and the hall was extended three times, ending with around 850 columns.
cordoba-mezquita-arches.caption:
The arches are a lower horseshoe and an upper semicircle, banded in red brick and pale stone. Cordoba fell to Castile in 1236 and the building became a cathedral, and in 1523 a Renaissance nave was cut into the middle of the hall. alhambra-no-victor-but-god.hook: One sentence is carved thousands of times across the Alhambra
lines: The Alhambra was built on a ridge above Granada by the Nasrid sultans, mostly between 1238 and 1391.
Running through its decoration, in courtyards and over doorways, is the Nasrid motto: there is no victor but Allah.
A dynasty that survived by paying tribute to Castile wrote it on every wall of the palace they lost in 1492.
alhambra-no-victor-but-god.caption:
Its walls are not carved stone but moulded plaster, cut and painted while damp, which is why so much detail was possible and why so much of it has had to be repaired. The motto appears in cursive and in angular script, and scholars who have counted the inscriptions put its repetitions in the thousands.

kairouan-great-mosque-minaret.hook: The oldest standing minaret is a square tower in Tunisia
lines: Uqba ibn Nafi founded Kairouan in 670 as a garrison in the Tunisian steppe.

qarawiyyin-library-fez.hook: One of the world's oldest working libraries reopened in 2016
lines: The library of the Qarawiyyin in Fez holds about four thousand manuscripts and has been in use since medieval times.
By 2012 it had broken gutters, damp in the walls and a collection at risk.
Aziza Chaouni, an engineer and architect from Fez, led the restoration, and it opened to readers again in 2016.

Among the manuscripts are a ninth century copy of Malik's Muwatta written on parchment and a fourteenth century copy of Ibn Khaldun's Muqaddimah. djenne-mud-mosque-replastering.hook: A whole town replasters its mosque in a single day
lines: The Great Mosque of Djenne in Mali is the largest mud brick building in the world.
Its walls are coated in banco, a mud and rice husk plaster that the rainy season washes away every year.
Each spring the town replasters it: masons direct, men carry the mud, women bring water, and it is done in one day.
djenne-mud-mosque-replastering.caption:
The masons belong to the local guild, and the bundles of palm wood that stick out of the walls, the toron, are the permanent scaffolding they climb. lines: In the fishing village of Kizimkazi, at the southern tip of Zanzibar, a small mosque carries a foundation inscription.

lines: The Great Mosque of Xi'an sits in the old Muslim quarter of the city, at the eastern end of what was the Silk Road.

lines: The Kalyan minaret in Bukhara was finished in 1127 for the Karakhanid ruler Arslan Khan, in baked brick.
It is about forty six metres high, worked into fourteen bands, each a different pattern laid up in the brick itself.
